chapter: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
title: Pops Foster refuses to play without him when he lacked a tuxedo
summary: At a small Village gig he was barred for not wearing a tux; Pops Foster threatened to pull the whole band out, and Autrey has loved him ever since.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So when you ran out, what happened this time? Where did you go from there?

Well, from there I went to -- I'm still staying in New York, and I went down to -- I hadn't met Charlie Johnson's band in Philadelphia before I came to New York, and bass man, who's gone now, the greatest bass player in the world --

Well Pops always did think a lot of me. He want -- he said Boy, come on in the band, but he's with Louie Russell then, so he wanted me in the band, and he said you should be here, you should be there, you should been -- so when I -- aw, I missing, when I did come to New York, I -- and got this room, I needed a job, I was hungry. They have no room, and I didn't have money to pay room rent, or anything, so somebody called me and gave me this job, I think it was four or five dollars, in the Village, and when I got there

they didn't -- well I had a tuxedo, but no one told me tuxedo, so I grabbed my trumpet and a dark suit and I ran on down there. So I got ready to get on the stand and the manager who ran the place, somebody, said Who are you?

I said I'm the trumpet player. Well where's your tux? I said well nobody told me to. He said well you can't get up on -- you can't get up there, you know. Well, I figure speak for four or five dollars (unintelligible) you know. Until you get the tux you can't get on that stand. Maybe he was waiter. I don't know who the heck he was. Pops walks in there, and I sat back there alone. What's the matter, boy? What's the matter, fellow? Huh? this man says I can't get up, I says (unintelligible). Why can't -- why -- what? Okay, if he doesn't get up, I don't get up. And that was it. And Pops sat packing up his bass. He said wait, Pop, wait, wait. I said well nobody told me to wear a tuxedo, so, and so, and see, so he says if this man goes home, I go home, and I'll pull the whole band out of here. So man, was I having a ride. I loved him after that, because my wife and I needed the money. We couldn't eat. I had no rent money, nothing to eat with, or anything. So that five bucks was really -- and Pops came in there with a tuxedo, stiff shirt, tie, oh man, he looked like he's going -- just walked out of the movies, or going to walk into the movies. You know.
Because he was with the big band there making money,
but he didn't know [Mike] and anyhow -- I guess he knew, but anyway, but he stood up for me, and I loved him until this day for that. You know?

Because he just said well, sorry sonny, you don't have a tux, goodbye, you know? later, you know. And I had to get -- I don't -- I doubt whethr I had over a nickel to get back there, the subway was a nickel then. I guess I had a nickel to get back uptown, maybe I did. I don't know if I had, but I got to done more -- you know. So that was it.
And I've never forgotten him for it, and --
